grade.rationale: The implementation is readable and uses atomic replacement for individual snapshot files, but it has a path-containment flaw, unsafe concurrent persistence, and failure modes that can silently lose or strand run data.

summary: Four substantive issues were identified: dot-segment run IDs can escape the intended run directory, concurrent operation writes can fail or lose observations, creation is not recoverable after partial failure, and malformed progress records are silently discarded regardless of position. Build analysis reported no findings; test coverage is unknown.

grade.rationale: Run IDs are not fully contained beneath the runs directory, concurrent writes can lose state, and interrupted creation can leave permanently incomplete runs.
The implementation is compact and factored into helpers, but persistence invariants and concurrency assumptions are implicit and duplicated across write paths.
Naming and record structures are clear, although the progress-recovery comment overstates what the implementation verifies.
Individual snapshot replacement is guarded with temporary-file cleanup, but partial creation is unrecoverable and progress corruption is suppressed without reporting.
The store can be exercised through temporary directories, but hardwired filesystem operations and absent synchronization abstractions make concurrency and failure-injection testing difficult.

findings.title: Dot-segment run IDs escape the runs directory
findings.description: The validation rejects directory separators but permits `.` and `..` because each can equal its own `Path.GetFileName` result. `Path.Combine(runsPath, "..")` resolves operations into the parent `.quality` directory, while `.` targets the runs root itself. Consequently, status and result writes can overwrite fixed-name files outside the intended per-run directory.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the candidate directory with `Path.GetFullPath`, verify that it is a strict child of the canonical runs path using the platform-appropriate comparison, and explicitly reject `.` and `..`. Prefer additionally restricting run IDs to a documented safe character set.

findings.title: Concurrent operation writes can fail or lose persisted state
findings.description: `AppendProgress` opens the shared JSONL file without write sharing, so simultaneous callers can receive sharing violations. `WriteObservation` performs an unsynchronized read-modify-replace sequence; two writers can read the same snapshot and each replace it, causing the later replacement to discard the other operation's observation. Atomic replacement prevents torn files but does not prevent lost updates.
findings.recommendation: Serialize all writes for a run using a per-run lock or a single writer. Alternatively, store each observation in its own create-or-replace file and use an append strategy with explicit interprocess synchronization for progress. Document whether synchronization must work across both threads and processes, then test that contract.

findings.title: Interrupted creation leaves a run that cannot be retried
findings.description: Creation exposes the run directory and writes the manifest, queued transitions, status, and result as separate operations. A crash or I/O failure after the create-only manifest write can leave an incomplete run that `LoadAll` skips. Retrying `Create` with the same run ID then fails because `manifest.json` already exists, so the API provides no way to complete or cleanly recover that run.
findings.recommendation: Stage the complete initial run in a uniquely named sibling directory and atomically rename it into place after all required files are durable. If that is not feasible, implement an explicit idempotent recovery protocol that validates and completes an existing partial run.

findings.title: Malformed progress records are silently discarded anywhere in the log
findings.description: Every `JsonException` is ignored, although the comment describes recovery only for an incomplete final record. Corruption or incompatible data in the middle of the file is therefore treated as an absent transition, potentially producing an inaccurate reconstructed run without invoking the supplied failure callback.
findings.recommendation: Determine the last non-empty record and tolerate malformed JSON only there when it is plausibly truncated. Treat malformed earlier records as invalid data, or return/report a structured warning so callers know the reconstructed progress is incomplete.
